section.title: Future Glory
section.sectionRationale: Having declared believers to be heirs who suffer with Christ, Paul now lifts their eyes to the glory that awaits. Present sufferings are not worth comparing with the coming glory. All creation groans like a woman in labor, waiting for the revealing of the sons of God, and believers groan too, awaiting the redemption of their bodies. In their weakness the Spirit intercedes with groans too deep for words, and behind it all stands the assurance that God works all things together for good, in an unbreakable chain from His eternal foreknowledge to the final glory of His people.
section.thesis: The sufferings of this present time cannot be compared with the glory to be revealed; creation and believers groan in hope while the Spirit intercedes, and God works all things together for the good of those He foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and will surely glorify.
section.frameNote: Four movements: present sufferings weighed against future glory; the groaning of creation in hope; the groaning of believers and the interceding Spirit; and the golden chain by which God works all things for good, from foreknowledge to glory.

verses.text: I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the {{doxa|glory}} that will be revealed in us.

units.label: Creation groaning in hope
units.note: awaiting the revealing of the sons of God

verses.text: The creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God.
For the creation was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope
that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God.
We know that the whole creation has been {{stenazo|groaning}} together in the pains of childbirth until the present time.

units.label: Believers groaning and the interceding Spirit
units.note: the firstfruits of the Spirit, hope, and help in weakness

verses.text: Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.
For in this {{elpis|hope}} we were saved; but hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what he can already see?
But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently.
In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words.
And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.

units.label: The golden chain, from foreknowledge to glory
units.note: God works all things together for good

verses.text: And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.
For those God {{proginosko|foreknew}}, He also {{proorizo|predestined}} to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers.
And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.

doxa.gloss: Glory, radiance, weight of splendor. It is the shining honor and likeness of God Himself, into which His children will be brought. Paul weighs all present suffering against this coming glory and finds no comparison; the glory to be revealed in us so far outweighs our afflictions that they seem light and momentary beside it.

stenazo.gloss: To groan, to sigh under a burden. Paul hears three groans in this passage: the groaning of creation in the pains of childbirth, the inward groaning of believers who await the redemption of their bodies, and the wordless groans of the Spirit interceding within them. The groan is not despair but the ache of hope, longing for the birth of the new world.

elpis.gloss: Hope, confident expectation of a certain future good. Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but sure assurance grounded in God's promise. In this hope believers were saved, and because it reaches to what is not yet seen, it is held with patient endurance while creation and the children of God await their freedom.

proginosko.gloss: To know beforehand. In Scripture God's knowing is often more than foresight of facts; it is His setting of covenant love upon persons, as when He says He knew Israel of all the families of the earth. Those God foreknew He marked out as His own before time, the first link in the unbreakable chain that ends in glory.

proorizo.gloss: To mark out beforehand, to predestine, to appoint in advance to a certain end. God predestined those He foreknew to be conformed to the image of His Son. The word secures that salvation begins in God's eternal purpose, not in human decision, and moves surely toward its appointed goal, the likeness of Christ and the sharing of His glory.

basic.context: Paul has just called believers heirs who suffer with Christ before being glorified with Him. Now he opens up that glory. The whole world is broken and groaning, and Christians groan too, but not without hope. The Spirit prays within us when we do not know how, and God is working every single thing toward the good of His people and their final glory.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as comfort for sufferers. Paul does not deny the pain; he weighs it against the coming glory and finds it light by comparison. The three groans, creation, believers, and the Spirit, hold together honesty about suffering and confidence in hope. The chain of verses 29 and 30 is meant to steady trembling hearts: what God begins in eternity He will surely finish in glory.
basic.originalLanguages: The coming splendor is doxa, glory, the weight of God's own radiance. The groaning is stenazo, the ache of creation, of believers, and of the Spirit. Believers were saved in elpis, sure hope for what is not yet seen. And the chain begins with those God did proginosko, foreknew, and proorizo, predestined, to be conformed to His Son.
basic.typology: The bondage of creation to decay recalls the ground cursed after the fall, and its coming freedom answers that curse. The firstfruits of the Spirit recalls the firstfruits offered to God as a pledge of the full harvest. The redemption of the body is the true and final exodus, the setting free of the whole person and the whole world from bondage.
basic.christ: The goal of predestination is to be conformed to the image of God's Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brothers. Christ is the pattern of the glory to come and the elder brother of the redeemed family. The Spirit who intercedes is His Spirit, and the good toward which all things work is our being made like Him and brought to share His glory.
basic.god: God is sovereign over suffering and history: He subjected creation in hope, He works all things together for good, and He carries His people from foreknowledge to glory without losing one. He is the God who searches hearts, hears the Spirit's intercession, and purposes the good of those who love Him, a good defined as likeness to His Son.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Corinthians 4 weighs light momentary affliction against an eternal weight of glory. Genesis 3 tells of the ground cursed, which creation's groaning recalls. Ephesians 1 speaks of being predestined in love before the foundation of the world. Philippians 1 promises that God will complete the work He began.
basic.oneStory: The whole creation has been groaning since the fall, longing to be set free. Paul tells the story's end: God is bringing many sons to glory, conformed to the image of His Son, and the redeemed creation itself will share their freedom. From God's eternal purpose to the final glory, the story cannot fail, for God Himself carries it through.

context.literary:
Romans 8:18-30 is built around three groans, and the repetition is the skeleton of the passage. Creation groans, verse 22. We groan, verse 23. The Spirit groans, verse 26. Each groan is followed by a statement of hope, so that the passage keeps turning from ache to assurance and back. Verse 18 states the thesis as a comparison, and the paragraph then explains it with a run of linked 'for' clauses: for creation waits, verse 19; for it was subjected, verse 20; for in this hope we were saved, verse 24. Paul is arguing, not merely consoling.

The ladder of verses 19 to 23 climbs through three circles. First the non-human creation, then 'we ourselves,' then in verse 26 the Spirit Himself, so that the groan reaches from the outermost edge of the cosmos to the inner life of God. The word 'hope' appears in verses 20, 24 and 25, and 'wait' in verses 19, 23 and 25, which makes patience the practical outcome of the whole.

Verses 28 to 30 shift to a different register. The 'we know' of verse 28 matches the 'we know' of verse 22, and what follows is a chain, with each link repeating the verb of the one before. The chain forms a staircase: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified. The last verb is in the past tense, though the glory is still future, which is Paul's way of treating the end as already secured. The passage then sets up the great questions of verses 31 to 39, which grow out of verse 30.
context.historical:
Paul writes from Corinth, probably in the mid fifties, to house churches in the capital. Christians in Rome were a minority in a city where public life was soaked in the worship of the emperor and the gods. The sufferings Paul has in mind in verse 18 are not abstract. The pairing of suffering with Christ in verse 17 and the list of hardships in verse 35 point to real social cost, from lost standing and business to the mob. Within a decade Nero would turn on the Roman believers, though Paul does not know that yet.

The picture of creation in 'the pains of childbirth' draws on a long Jewish habit of describing the end of the age as birth pangs, a world in labor before the new one arrives. The prophets used birth imagery for coming judgment and for coming deliverance, as in Isaiah 26:17-18 and Micah 4:9-10. Jesus used the same picture in Mark 13:8. Paul's first readers would have heard that the groaning marks the approach of the birth, not the failure of the world.

The vocabulary of 'adoption' and 'redemption' would also have carried weight in Rome. Adoption was a familiar legal act that gave an adopted son the full standing of an heir. 'Redemption' was the language of the marketplace and of release from bondage. Paul sets both in a future key: the adoption has been received, verse 15, and is still awaited in its fullness, verse 23.
context.canonical:
The passage reaches back to Genesis 3, where God said to Adam, 'cursed is the ground because of you,' Genesis 3:17. Paul's 'subjected to futility' in verse 20 is the New Testament's commentary on that curse, and the phrase 'not by its own will' lays the blame on the human act that caused it, while 'because of the One who subjected it' lays the sentence on God. The 'futility' recalls Ecclesiastes, where the Preacher finds all things under the sun wearisome and vain, Ecclesiastes 1:2.

Forward from the curse, the Old Testament holds out a renewed creation. Isaiah promises that the wolf will dwell with the lamb and that the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD, Isaiah 11:6-9, and speaks of new heavens and a new earth, Isaiah 65:17. Paul reads these as the other side of verse 21. Peter echoes the hope, 2 Peter 3:13, and Revelation completes it with 'No longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3.

The theme of present suffering weighed against coming glory runs through the New Testament. Paul says it again in 2 Corinthians 4:17, Peter in 1 Peter 5:10, and Jesus in the Beatitudes. The chain of verses 29 and 30 has its twin in Ephesians 1:4-5 and 1:11, and its goal in Philippians 3:21, where Christ will 'transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.' The Spirit who intercedes is the Spirit of verses 9 to 16, and Hebrews 7:25 and Romans 8:34 say the Son does the same, so the whole Trinity pleads for the saints.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant his readers to hold two things together that suffering tempts us to separate. The first is realism. He does not say that pain is an illusion or that faith removes it, and he repeats the word groan three times. The second is hope with substance behind it, grounded in what God has already done in giving the Spirit as firstfruits, verse 23. He wants suffering Christians to see their pain as part of a story that is heading somewhere, the way labor pains belong to a birth.

He also means to widen their horizon. The believers in Rome had a personal salvation, but Paul tells them their future is bound to the future of the whole creation. The glory is not only an escape from the world but the renewal of it, so the hope is bigger than the individual.

Finally, he gives them a way to keep praying when words fail. Verse 26 is written for the believer who sits in silence, unable to name what to ask. The answer is not a technique but a Person. The chain of verses 29 and 30 is then a pastoral anchor and not a puzzle for speculation: whoever is in Christ is held by a purpose that began before time and cannot stop short of glory.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this passage describes what God has done and will do, and it is meant to be believed and not obeyed. The groaning of creation, the Spirit's intercession and the chain of verses 29 and 30 are statements of fact about God's work. The only direct posture Paul draws out is patient waiting, verse 25. It would be a misreading to turn the passage into a rule that Christians must suppress their grief, or must feel glad about their suffering. Paul himself groans.

Verse 28 is the verse most often lifted out and applied wrongly. It is a promise to a particular people, 'those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose,' and it is not a claim that every event is good in itself. Nor does it say that every outcome will be pleasant. The 'good' is defined in verse 29 as conformity to the Son, so the promise guarantees the direction of the believer's life, not the comfort of any given chapter of it.

What carries forward as practice is honest prayer, even wordless prayer, together with patient hope. The passage releases believers from the pressure to pray perfectly, since the Spirit is already praying for them.

debates.question: What is the 'creation' that groans in verses 19 to 22?

views.label: The whole non-human creation
views.case: Paul says the creation was subjected 'in hope' that 'the creation itself' will be set free into the freedom of the children of God, verses 20 and 21. The phrase 'the creation itself' is set apart from believers in verse 23, 'Not only that, but we ourselves.' Read together with Genesis 3:17 and Isaiah 11:6-9, this makes the natural world the subject. Most interpreters since the early church have taken it this way.

views.label: Unbelieving humanity
views.case: Some older writers took the creation to mean the unsaved human world, since only people can wait eagerly or be set free. They argue that rocks and rivers cannot hope.

views.label: Angels or the whole cosmos including the powers
views.case: A few have included spiritual beings. The text gives little to support this, and verse 38 treats angels and powers separately.

debates.bearing: The weight of the language, with its subjection, bondage to decay and childbirth, falls most naturally on the physical world, which is a personification in the way the Psalms call the trees to sing, Psalm 96:12. The practical result is the same either way: the redemption of believers and the renewal of the world are bound up together.

debates.question: How should foreknowledge and predestination in verse 29 be understood?

views.label: God foreknew people in the sense of knowing them in love beforehand
views.case: The verb takes people, 'those God foreknew,' not facts or future faith. Scripture uses 'know' for covenant love, as in Amos 3:2 and Jeremiah 1:5, and Paul speaks of those 'known by God' in Galatians 4:9. The chain makes foreknowledge the first link of a work God carries out, and Paul does not name faith as its cause.

views.label: God foresaw who would believe and chose them on that basis
views.case: The verse says God foreknew before predestining, and some conclude that foreseen faith is the ground. They point to 1 Peter 1:2, where election is 'according to the foreknowledge of God the Father.'

views.label: Predestination is of a corporate people in Christ
views.case: Others stress that the destination is conformity to the Son, and that God chose a people in Him, Ephesians 1:4. Individuals enter that people by faith.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on the point Paul is making, that no one in the chain is lost: the same people foreknown are glorified. The text itself aims to steady the believer and does not open a seminar on how God's purposes relate to human choices. Chapters 9 and 10 return to the question.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 18 begins with a verb of accounting, logizomai, 'I consider,' the same verb that Paul used for crediting righteousness in Romans 4. Here it describes the careful reckoning of a person who has weighed the two sides. The comparison is that sufferings are 'not comparable,' literally not worth setting beside the glory. The glory is 'revealed in us,' and the preposition can carry the sense 'to us' or 'in us.' The idea is of something hidden that will be unveiled, which links to the noun in verse 19, apokalypsis, 'revelation,' used for the unveiling of the sons of God.

The most unusual word of verse 19 is apokaradokia, 'eager expectation.' It is built from words that picture the head stretched forward, looking intently at the horizon. The only other place Paul uses the word is Philippians 1:20, where he waits with the same eager expectation to be unashamed in Christ. Creation is pictured with its neck craned toward the day of the sons of God.

The word translated 'futility' in verse 20 is mataiotes. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the 'vanity' of Ecclesiastes, so Paul places the groaning world under the verdict of the Preacher. The verb 'subjected' is in the passive, and the agent is named in the phrase 'the One who subjected it,' which must be God, since Adam could not subject the creation to anything. Then comes 'in hope,' which can be read with the verb of subjection, so that God judged the world with a view to restoring it.

Verse 22 uses two compounds with the sense of 'together': sustenazo, groaning together, and synodino, being in labor together. The 'together' ties the whole creation into one shared pang. In verse 23 the 'firstfruits' is aparche, the first portion of the harvest, which belongs to God and pledges the rest. The Spirit is the firstfruits because He is the down payment on the full harvest of the redeemed body.

Verse 26 says the Spirit 'helps' us. The verb is synantilambanomai, which means taking hold of a burden together with someone from the opposite side, as two people carry a beam. Luke uses the same verb only once, in Luke 10:40, where Martha asks that her sister help her. The Spirit 'intercedes' with a compound form of the verb that appears in verse 27 and verse 34, where Christ is said to intercede. The groans are 'too deep for words,' and the adjective can mean either unspoken or unspeakable.

In verse 28 the verb 'works together' is synergeo. The Greek can be read with 'God' as subject, as in the BSB, or with 'all things' as subject, and the sense is almost the same. The 'purpose' is prothesis, the settled plan, which returns in 9:11. In verse 30 each verb is in the aorist tense, including 'glorified.' The aorist of a future event is Paul's way of presenting it as certain.

typology.type: The birth pangs of a woman in labor, Romans 8:22
typology.fulfillment: Prophets and Jesus pictured the end of the age as labor, pain that ends in a birth, Isaiah 26:17-18 and Mark 13:8. Paul applies it to the whole creation and to believers, who groan toward the delivery of a renewed world and renewed bodies. The correspondence is that the pain is purposeful and temporary. It escalates in Christ, who first passed through the pangs of death and became 'the firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18, and so guarantees the birth that follows. The picture falls short because a mother's pain is naturally followed by a child, while here the child is a new creation that only God can bring.

typology.type: The firstfruits of the Spirit, Romans 8:23
typology.fulfillment: Israel brought the first sheaf of the harvest to God as a sign that the whole crop belonged to Him and was coming, Leviticus 23:10-11. The Spirit given now is the sheaf that pledges the full harvest, the redeemed body. The pattern finds its center in Christ, 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, whose resurrection is the first sheaf of the great harvest, with believers following in order, 1 Corinthians 15:23. The type is imperfect in that an offering was laid on an altar, while the Spirit is given inwardly and personally, dwelling in His people as a pledge, Ephesians 1:13-14.

typology.type: Creation set free from bondage, Romans 8:21
typology.fulfillment: Israel was brought out of Egypt from bondage to freedom, and the prophets pictured a second and greater release, including a restored land and earth, Isaiah 11:6-9 and Isaiah 35:1-2. Paul now speaks of a release from 'bondage to decay' for the whole created order. The pattern escalates because the slavery is not political but cosmic, and the deliverer is Christ, through whom 'all things' are reconciled, Colossians 1:20. The correspondence stops short in that the earlier exodus freed a nation within history, while this one frees the world from death itself, at the revealing of the sons of God, Revelation 21:1-5.

typology.type: The Spirit who intercedes and the Son who intercedes, Romans 8:26 and 8:34
typology.fulfillment: Israel's high priest stood before God on behalf of the people with their names on his shoulders and breastplate, Exodus 28:9-12 and 28:29. The saints now have a Priest who lives forever to make intercession, Hebrews 7:25, and a Spirit who prays within them. The correspondence is of mediation on behalf of the weak. Christ escalates it by pleading in heaven, and the Spirit pleads in the heart. The type falls short because the old priest was sinful and mortal, Hebrews 7:27-28, while this intercession is never interrupted, and never fails because it is according to the will of God, verse 27.

study.christ:
Romans 8:18-30 leads to Christ most plainly through its goal. The purpose of God in verse 29 is that believers be 'conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers.' Everything in the paragraph is aimed at that: the groaning, the waiting, the redemption of bodies, the good that all things work toward. The image of Christ is the shape of our final glory, and Paul spells out what that shape is in Philippians 3:21 and 1 Corinthians 15:49, where we bear 'the likeness of the heavenly man.' The word 'firstborn' recalls Colossians 1:15 and 1:18, where Christ is firstborn of creation and firstborn from the dead. He is the first of a family, and the rest follow Him.

The passage leads to Christ by the pattern of suffering before glory. Verse 17 says believers suffer with Him in order to be glorified with Him, and the same road is the one He walked, Luke 24:26, 'Did not the Christ have to suffer these things and then enter into His glory?' The sufferings of verse 18 are therefore not a sign that God has left His people but the mark that they are traveling with their Lord. Peter draws the same line in 1 Peter 4:13 and 5:10.

It leads to Christ in the Spirit's work. The Spirit is called 'the Spirit of Christ' in verse 9, and the intercession in verse 26 goes alongside Christ's own intercession at the right hand of God, verse 34. The believer is never praying alone, because the Son pleads above and the Spirit within.

It leads to Christ through creation. Paul says all things were created through and for Him, Colossians 1:16, and that He will reconcile all things to Himself, Colossians 1:20. The liberation of creation in verse 21 is the restoration of His own world under His rule, Ephesians 1:10.

It is worth guarding against forced allegory. The passage does not say that the groaning of the world is a hidden picture of Christ's passion, and it is unwise to find His cross in every labor pain. What Paul does say is that the glory ahead is His glory shared, and that the pangs of the present are the pangs that precede His appearing. The link is a plain one of promise and pattern, which is firm enough.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is His sovereignty over a broken world. Creation was subjected 'in hope' by God Himself, verse 20, so even the curse is not outside His hand and belongs to His design. He did not lose control when Adam sinned, and He did not give up the creation. Sovereignty here is not cold control but is joined to purpose and to hope.

He is a God who weighs suffering and glory in His own balance. The comparison of verse 18 is not a denial that pain is real but an assessment from the one who knows both. Scripture elsewhere calls the glory 'eternal' and the affliction 'momentary,' 2 Corinthians 4:17, and only God sees the full scale.

He is God the Father who 'searches our hearts,' verse 27, a title taken from the Old Testament, where the LORD alone searches hearts, 1 Chronicles 28:9 and Jeremiah 17:10. He knows 'the mind of the Spirit,' which shows the Spirit to be a Person with a mind, distinct from the Father, and that the Father and the Spirit understand one another perfectly. The intercession is 'according to the will of God,' so God hears prayers that arise from His own Spirit.

He is a God who involves all three Persons in the believer's salvation. The Father foreknows, predestines and calls, the Son is the image to which we are conformed and who intercedes, and the Spirit is the firstfruits and the intercessor. Salvation is not one divine act but an undivided work of the Trinity.

He is faithful from beginning to end. The chain of verse 30 has no breaks, and the number of those glorified is the same as the number justified. That is a statement about God's reliability and not an invitation to presumption. Because the work belongs to Him, it cannot fail through human weakness.

He is also a God who suffers with His people in a way. The Spirit groans, and Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, John 11:35. This does not make God weak, but it shows that His nearness to the suffering is real.

For worship, the passage gives believers permission to be honest and to wait. Praise in this life is mixed with groaning, and the Lord is not offended by that mixture. It points to the day when the groaning is turned into song, Revelation 21:4.

crossReferences.note: Paul weighs the same scales again, calling the affliction 'light and momentary' and the glory an 'eternal weight.' He adds that the way to hold both is to fix our eyes on what is unseen, which matches the logic of Romans 8:24-25, where hope for what we cannot yet see is what makes us wait.

The sentence on the ground is the origin of the bondage Paul mentions. Because of Adam's sin the soil yields thorns and thistles and the man toils until he returns to dust. Romans 8:20-21 reads that curse as temporary, subjected 'in hope.'

A picture of the creation freed from violence, with the wolf living with the lamb and the earth full of the knowledge of the LORD. It is the Old Testament form of the hope Paul calls the 'glorious freedom of the children of God,' and it shows that the renewal of nature is a prophetic promise and not a novelty.

The Spirit is described as a down payment on our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession. It makes the same point as the 'firstfruits' of Romans 8:23: what we have now is a real first installment of what is to come.

Christ is raised as the firstfruits, and those who belong to Him follow at His coming. It supplies the content behind 'the redemption of our bodies' in Romans 8:23, which is bodily resurrection on the pattern of His.

Christ 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near to God through Him. It sits beside Romans 8:26 and 8:34 and shows that the believer is supported by two intercessors, the Spirit within and the Son above.

Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body, by the power that subjects all things to Himself. It explains what being 'conformed to the image of His Son' means for the body, and so what the glory of Romans 8:18 consists of.

Paul sets election and adoption in the opening blessing of Ephesians, 'in love,' before time began. It shows that the 'predestined' of Romans 8:29 is set within the love of the Father and not in a cold decree, and the goal in both is sonship.

Paul is sure that He who began a good work in the Philippians will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. It is the same confidence as the unbroken chain of Romans 8:30, applied to a single congregation.
A new heaven and a new earth, God dwelling with His people, and every tear wiped away. This is where the groaning of Romans 8:22-23 ends, with the former things passing away and everything made new.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a world pronounced good and ends with a world made new, and Romans 8:18-30 is the passage that explains the long middle in between. The groaning Paul describes started in Genesis 3 and has run through every chapter since, through the toil of Adam's descendants, the slavery in Egypt, the exile, and the cross itself. The Old Testament never explains why the creation should still be in labor, and here Paul gives the reason and the promise together: the creation was subjected in hope.

The passage also looks back to the promise made in Eden, that a seed of the woman would undo what the serpent had done, Genesis 3:15. The 'firstborn among many brothers' is that seed, and the brothers are those joined to Him. It looks back as well to Israel's story. The adoption, the glory and the promises, which Romans 9:4 lists as Israel's, are here being extended to a people drawn from every nation, while the exodus pattern of redemption from bondage is lifted to the scale of the cosmos.

Looking forward, the passage sets up everything that remains in Romans. The questions of 8:31 to 39 are asked from the high ground of verse 30. Chapters 9 to 11 will ask how Israel fits into the chain of calling and glory, and chapters 12 to 16 will describe how the people who wait for this glory live in the meantime.

The ending is set out in the closing chapters of Revelation. The creation that groaned is replaced by a new heaven and a new earth, the curse is lifted, death is destroyed, and the sons of God are revealed in glory, Revelation 21:1-4 and 22:3. Until then, believers live in the present between the firstfruits and the harvest, carried by the Spirit who prays with them and by the Son who prays for them, in a story whose last page has already been written.

quiz.q: How does Paul weigh present sufferings against future glory?

options.text: Present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us.
options.note: Verse 18 declares the coming glory so great that suffering cannot be weighed against it.

options.text: Present sufferings and future glory are roughly equal.
options.note: Closer: they can be set side by side, but Paul says they are not comparable, the glory far outweighing the suffering.

options.text: Present sufferings prove that God has abandoned His people.
options.note: Paul treats suffering as the path to glory, not a sign of abandonment.

options.text: Future glory is uncertain and may never come.
options.note: The glory is certain; the whole passage rests on its sure hope.

quiz.q: Why does creation groan, according to Paul?

options.text: It was subjected to futility in hope, and groans in the pains of childbirth awaiting its freedom.
options.note: Verses 20 to 22 describe creation groaning in hope for its coming liberation.

options.text: It groans in final despair, with no hope of renewal.
options.note: Closer: the groaning is real, but it is in hope; creation will be set free from bondage to decay.

options.text: It groans because matter is inherently evil.
options.note: Creation is not evil but subjected to futility, and it will be renewed, not destroyed.

options.text: It does not really groan; this is only a figure with no meaning.
options.note: Paul teaches a real longing of creation for the revealing of the sons of God.

quiz.q: How does the Spirit help believers in their weakness?

options.text: He intercedes for them with groans too deep for words, according to the will of God.
options.note: Verses 26 and 27 describe the Spirit's intercession when we do not know how to pray.

options.text: He removes all weakness so that prayer becomes easy.
options.note: The Spirit helps us in our weakness rather than abolishing it.

options.text: He prays instead of us so that we need not pray at all.
options.note: Closer: the Spirit truly intercedes, but He helps alongside our praying, not in place of it.

options.text: He leaves believers to manage their prayers on their own.
options.note: The whole point is that the Spirit Himself intercedes for us.

quiz.q: What is the good that God works all things together for?

options.text: The good of being conformed to the image of His Son and finally glorified.
options.note: Verse 29 defines the good as conformity to Christ, the goal of God's purpose.

options.text: A comfortable life free from all hardship.
options.note: Closer: God does work for our good, but the good is Christlikeness and glory, not ease, since the context is suffering.

options.text: Immediate success in every earthly endeavor.
options.note: The good is defined by the passage as likeness to Christ, not worldly success.

options.text: Nothing in particular; the phrase is only a comforting slogan.
options.note: Paul gives it precise content: conformity to the Son and final glory.

quiz.q: What is the golden chain of verses 29 and 30?

options.text: Those God foreknew He predestined, called, justified, and glorified, an unbroken saving purpose.
options.note: The five verbs carry God's people from eternity to glory without loss.

options.text: A series of steps believers must climb by their own effort.
options.note: God is the actor in every link; it is His work, not human striving.

options.text: A chain that can be broken at any point by failure.
options.note: Closer: the chain is real, but it is unbroken; all whom God foreknew He also glorified.

options.text: A promise that applies only to the apostles.
options.note: It applies to all who love God and are called according to His purpose.

questions: Paul says present sufferings are not worth comparing with the coming glory. How would keeping that comparison before you change the way you carry a present hardship?
All creation groans in hope for renewal. How does it enlarge your hope to know that God will not scrap the world but set it free from bondage to decay?
The Spirit intercedes for you with groans too deep for words. What comfort is there in knowing that even when you cannot pray, the Spirit is praying within you according to God's will?
God works all things together for the good of conforming you to Christ. Where do you need to trust that even painful things are being woven toward that good?
From foreknowledge to glory, God loses none of His own. How does the certainty of that chain steady you when your assurance feels shaky?

translationNotes.note: Futility renders a word meaning emptiness or frustration, the inability of creation to reach its intended purpose under the curse. Because of the One who subjected it points to God, who subjected creation not in anger only but in hope of its coming renewal.

God works all things together for good can also be read all things work together for good; the better attested reading makes God the active worker. The good is not ease but the conformity to Christ named in verse 29.

Foreknew renders proginosko; in biblical usage God's knowing often means His covenantal setting of love upon persons, not merely foresight of facts. Predestined renders proorizo, to mark out beforehand for an appointed end, here conformity to the image of His Son.
